name: Setswana
family: Niger-Congo, Atlantic-Congo, Bantu (Sotho-Tswana group, Guthrie S.31)
variety: Setswana as described for South African speakers from Taung and Kuruman (Bennett et al. 2016), with reference to the Botswana standard (Cole 1955; University of Botswana 2001)
sources: Bennett, Wm. G., Diemer, Maxine, Kerford, Justine, Probert, Tracy & Wesi, Tsholofelo (2016). Setswana (South African). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 46(2), 235-246.
Cole, Desmond T. (1955). An Introduction to Tswana Grammar. London: Longmans, Green.
Chebanne, Andy, Creissels, Denis & Nkhwa, H. W. (1997). Tonal Morphology of the Setswana Verb. München: LINCOM Europa.
University of Botswana (2001). The Sound System of Setswana. Gaborone: Lightbooks.
Le Roux, Mia & Le Roux, Jurie (2008). An acoustic assessment of Setswana vowels. South African Journal of African Languages 28, 156-171.
Gouskova, Maria, Zsiga, Elizabeth & Tlale Boyer, One (2011). Grounded constraints and the consonants of Setswana. Lingua 121, 2120-2152.
Coetzee, Andries W. & Pretorius, Rigardt (2010). Phonetically grounded phonology and sound change: the case of Tswana labial plosives. Journal of Phonetics 38, 404-421.
Schubö, F., Bekker, I., Pretorius, R., Wagner, V. & Zerbian, S. (2022). An exploration into penultimate and final lengthening in Tswana (Southern Bantu). Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62.
Zerbian, Sabine (2006). Questions in Northern Sotho. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 43, 257-280.
Maddieson, Ian (2003). The sounds of the Bantu languages. In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages. London: Routledge.
contrasts: seven vowel qualities in four heights; the letters e and o each spell two phonemes (ɪ and ɛ, ʊ and ɔ)
unaspirated (variably ejective) versus aspirated voiceless stops and affricates: p pʰ, t tʰ, k kʰ, ts tsʰ, tʃ tʃʰ, tɬ tɬʰ
lateral affricates tɬ and tɬʰ (written tl, tlh)
uvular fricative χ (written g) and uvular affricate qχ (written kg); there is no voiced velar stop
single versus doubled sonorants: mona 'jealousy' versus monna 'man'
high versus low tone, both lexical and grammatical
allophony: the unaspirated stops and affricates may be ejective [pʼ tʼ kʼ tsʼ tʃʼ tɬʼ]; one of three speakers in Bennett et al. (2016) did this consistently, and tɬ is the most clearly ejective
tɬʰ has less aspiration than tsʰ and tʃʰ
/l/ is [d] before the high vowels /i u/ (written d) and [l] elsewhere, including before raised mid vowels
/b/ may be made without full closure, as [β]
/χ/ varies between a uvular fricative, a voiceless uvular trill, velar [x] and [h]; older descriptions call it velar /x/
after a nasal prefix /χ/ hardens to [qχ], /s/ to [tsʰ], /ʃ/ to [tʃʰ], /h/ to [kʰ] or [pʰ], /r/ to [tʰ] and /l/ to [t]
/qχ/ is described as an aspirated velar affricate [kxʰ] or aspirated uvular stop [qʰ] in other sources
/f/ alternates with /h/ in many words and is bilabial [ɸ] in some dialects
mid vowels are raised before a syllable with a higher vowel, before s ʃ ts tsʰ tʃ tʃʰ tɬ tɬʰ ɲ and before locative -ŋ: /ɛ ɔ/ become [e o], /ɪ ʊ/ come close to [i u]
word-final vowels are often devoiced or centralised at the end of a phrase
/h/ between vowels is weakened or dropped
/r/ is a trill with two to three contacts, six to eight when doubled
a non-phonemic glottal stop may begin vowel-initial morphemes
word-final /ŋ/ takes the place of a following consonant in connected speech
syllable_structure: V, CV, CwV and syllabic sonorant (N̩, l̩, r̩); open syllables only
phonotactics: a nasal before another consonant is syllabic and homorganic, and bears tone
doubled sonorants (mm, nn, ŋŋ, ll, rr, as in mma, nnɛ, rrɛ) are a syllabic sonorant plus an onset
consonant plus w onsets are common (tsw, tshw, kw, ngw); labial consonants are avoided before w
[d] occurs only before i and u

clicks are not phonemes of Setswana (Maddieson 2003 lists Tswana among the southern Bantu languages without clicks; Bennett et al. 2016 give none); a dental, an alveolar and a lateral click, written c, q, x, are reported only for a few interjections and ideophones of older speakers

stress.type: fixed penultimate prominence, realised as lengthening
stress.rule: The penultimate syllable of a word, above all of the last word of a prosodic phrase, is lengthened and heard as stressed; there is no lexical stress contrast.
stress.cues: duration of the penultimate vowel or syllabic sonorant; pitch is used for tone. Inside a phrase the penultimate vowel is only about 14 percent longer than the final vowel (83 versus 73 ms, Schubö et al. 2022).

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in the lexicon; phrase-final vowels may be devoiced or centralised
rhythm.notes: At the end of a phrase both the penultimate and the final vowel lengthen by about 60 percent compared with phrase-medial position (penultimate vowel +51 ms, final vowel +43 ms; Schubö et al. 2022, six speakers). Bennett et al. (2016) report a difference of about 70 ms for a penultimate vowel in citation forms and more lengthening utterance-finally than phrase-finally inside an utterance. The rhythm class is assumed from the CV syllable structure; I know of no published rhythm metrics.

length.notes: Vowel length is not lexical; penultimate lengthening is predictable. Doubled sonorants in penultimate position are about three times as long as single ones (n 99 ms versus nn 310 ms, and 137 versus 437 ms, Bennett et al. 2016).

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Bennett et al. 2016, Table 1: duration from burst to vowel onset, three tokens each, one speaker

intonation.declarative: tones are realised on a falling register (downdrift); the last word has penultimate lengthening, and its final vowel is often devoiced
intonation.yes_no_question: same word order as a statement, optionally with the initial particle a; in the closely related Northern Sotho polar questions have raised overall pitch and lack penultimate lengthening (Zerbian 2006)
intonation.wh_question: question words (mang, eng, kae, jang) stay in place; no special contour is described in the sources consulted
intonation.continuation: phrase-final words inside an utterance keep a shorter penultimate lengthening (half length)
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; the pitch contour is the sequence of lexical and grammatical tones
intonation.notes: At the start of an utterance high and low tones may begin at the same pitch; low falls, high stays level or rises (Bennett et al. 2016).

inventory.name: high
inventory.description: high; holds its level or rises slightly

inventory.name: low
inventory.description: low, the more frequent tone; realised with a fall from the preceding level

sandhi: a high tone spreads rightwards onto following syllables, limited by the end of the word and phrase
downdrift lowers each high tone that follows a low tone
rising and falling contours arise when a high and a low tone meet on one lengthened syllable
verb forms and subject markers are distinguished by tone alone: o bina 'you dance' has a low subject marker, o bina 'she or he dances' a high one
tone.neutral_tone: none; every syllable, including a syllabic nasal, is high or low
tone.notes: Tone is not written in the standard orthography, so it cannot be recovered from text without a dictionary and a grammar of the verb. The Chao values are a conversion of high and low for a two-level system, not measured values.

phonation: ejective realisation of unaspirated voiceless stops and affricates (speaker-dependent)

problems: no tone at all: the phoneme table has no tone phonemes and the dictionary carries no tone marks, so lexical and grammatical high and low tones are lost
unstressed e is changed to the consonant l (ChangeIfUnstressed(l) in phoneme e, apparently a slip for a vowel): bogobe comes out as [βʊɡoβl], lefatshe as [llfatʃl]
g, which spells the fricative /χ/, is pronounced as the voiced stop [ɡ]; kg, which spells /qχ/, is pronounced [kɡ]
th and kh are read as the fricatives [θ] and [x], as in the Swahili rules the file was copied from, instead of aspirated /tʰ/ and /kʰ/
tsh is read as [tʃ] instead of /tsʰ/; š is read as [s]
tl is read as the fricative [ɬ] instead of the affricate /tɬ/
ng is read as [ŋɡ], also word-finally (jang) and before w (ngwana), where Setswana has [ŋ]
the seven-vowel system is not represented: e and o are given one quality each, with o becoming [ʊ] when unstressed, regardless of the lexical vowel
e after s is read as [i] (Setswana comes out as [sitswana]) and u after word-initial d is lengthened (dumela as [duːmela]), without basis in the language
the marginal clicks written c, q, x are read as k, k, ks
good: prominence and extra length on the penultimate syllable
syllabic nasals before consonants (mma, nna, ntša)
a separate phoneme for tlh, and aspirated ph

notes: Bennett et al. (2016) write the vowels /ɪ ʊ/ as raised close-mid [e̝ o̝]; Le Roux & Le Roux (2008) give formant measurements, which I could not check and therefore do not reproduce. Some descriptions count nine vowels because raised [e o] also occur where no raising trigger is present.
